question: In 1972, Atari released the first commercial video-game hit — a black-and-white tennis game with two paddles and a square ball. What was the game called?
context: Designed by Allan Alcorn under Atari co-founders Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney. The first prototype was installed at Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale CA in 1972 and broke down from too many coins jammed in the slot.

question: The 1980 Namco arcade hero who chomps dots in a maze while fleeing four colored ghosts is what color?
context: Pac-Man's round shape came from designer Toru Iwatani looking at a pizza with one slice missing. The four ghosts are Blinky (red), Pinky (pink), Inky (cyan), and Clyde (orange).

question: In Nintendo's 1981 arcade hit Donkey Kong, a giant ape kidnaps a maiden and climbs to the top of a construction site. The hero throws hammers and dodges barrels. What's the ape's name?
context: Designer Shigeru Miyamoto picked 'Donkey' to mean stubborn in English; the title literally means 'Stubborn Ape.' The hero, originally called Jumpman, was renamed Mario in 1982.

question: Sega's 1991 Genesis mascot is a fast hedgehog who collects gold rings and stops Dr Robotnik. What color is he?
context: Designer Naoto Ohshima chose blue to match Sega's logo. The shoes were inspired by Michael Jackson's Bad-album cover and Santa Claus boots.

question: Nintendo's 1985 NES launch hero wears blue overalls, a red shirt, and a red cap with the letter M on the front. Name him.
context: Super Mario Bros launched the modern console era in North America after the 1983 crash. Miyamoto picked the overalls and cap so animators could distinguish Mario's arms and hair on the limited NES sprite.

question: In Nintendo's Legend of Zelda series, the elf-eared boy hero in green tunic and cap fights Ganon. What's his name?
context: Designer Shigeru Miyamoto named him Link because he is the link between worlds. Zelda — the princess — was named after F. Scott Fitzgerald's wife Zelda Fitzgerald.

question: Nintendo's 1986 NES game Metroid stars a bounty hunter in orange armor exploring a hostile planet. What's the hunter's name?
context: Players who beat the original Metroid in under five hours saw the iconic reveal that Samus was a woman underneath the suit — one of the first major female protagonists in console gaming.

question: Pokemon's mascot is a yellow electric rodent who lives on Ash Ketchum's shoulder and shocks enemies. Name him.
context: Pokemon Red and Blue launched in Japan in 1996 and reached the US in September 1998. The anime made Pikachu Ash's starter to maximize merchandise appeal.

question: Namco's 1981 fixed-shooter sequel to Galaxian features colored alien insects in formation, a tractor beam that captures your ship, and bonus stages. Name it.
context: Recovering a captured ship from the tractor-beam alien doubles your firepower. Galaga famously cameos in Marvel's Avengers (2012) when an unnamed S.H.I.E.L.D. employee is caught playing it on his console.

question: A 1984 Soviet puzzle game featuring seven different falling block shapes that the player rotates and stacks into complete rows became the killer app for Nintendo's Game Boy. Name it.
context: Created by Alexey Pajitnov at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. Nintendo bundled it with every Game Boy at the 1989 US launch — selling Tetris to your grandma was the strategy.

question: The 1977 woodgrain-front home console that brought arcade games into the living room had a single joystick with one red button. Which company made it?
context: The Atari 2600 sold over 30 million units and was the dominant US console until the 1983 crash. Its game library included Combat, Pac-Man, E.T., and Pitfall!.

question: Nintendo's 1989 portable console had a green-tinted LCD screen, a D-pad, A/B buttons, Start/Select, and a Tetris cartridge in the box. What was the system called?
context: Designed by Gunpei Yokoi (also the creator of Metroid and Mario Maker concepts). The Game Boy's monochrome display and AA-battery efficiency crushed the technologically superior Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear.

question: Sony's 1994 gray CD-based console came with a controller featuring four shape buttons — triangle, circle, square, and X. Name the system.
context: The PlayStation began life as a Nintendo-Sony CD-add-on for the SNES; when Nintendo backed out in 1991, Sony took the hardware solo. The PS1 sold over 100 million units.

question: Microsoft's 2001 console launched with a sci-fi shooter featuring a green-armored super-soldier named Master Chief. What was the console called?
context: The Xbox was nicknamed the Direct X-box for its underlying graphics API. Halo: Combat Evolved was the killer app — Bungie's first-person shooter that defined console FPS controls.

question: Midway's 1992 arcade fighter features digitized real-actor sprites, a kick-and-punch fight system, and signature gory finishing moves. Name the move category that lets you brutally execute a defeated opponent.
context: Mortal Kombat's Fatalities triggered the US Senate hearings that led to the ESRB rating system in 1994. The Genesis port preserved the blood with the ABACABB code; the SNES port stripped it out.

question: Capcom's 1991 arcade hit Street Fighter II features a Japanese karate hero in white gi with a red headband whose signature blue-energy projectile is called what?
context: Performed by quarter-circle forward + punch. Hadoken means 'surging-wave fist.' Ryu's rival Ken (red gi, blond) shares the move. Both characters' costumes were designed by Akira Yasuda.

question: A 1987 NES RPG that the creator believed would be his last game before his company went bankrupt instead saved the company and launched one of the most famous series in gaming. Name the series.
context: Hironobu Sakaguchi at Square named it 'Final Fantasy' because if it failed it would be his final fantasy and he would quit gaming for med school. It sold 400,000 copies in Japan and saved Square.

question: In Nintendo's Legend of Zelda series, the kingdom Link explores and Princess Zelda rules over is called what?
context: Hyrule's geography shifts between games. The Triforce — three golden triangles representing Power, Wisdom, and Courage — is the source of magic in Hyrule. Ganon seeks Power, Zelda holds Wisdom, Link bears Courage.

question: Sony's 1996 PlayStation mascot is an orange marsupial in blue jeans who runs forward through islands smashing crates and spinning enemies. Name him.
context: Created by Naughty Dog's Jason Rubin and Andy Gavin. Sony used him as the unofficial mascot to challenge Mario and Sonic during the 32-bit era. He never spoke a real language — just yelled 'WOAH!'.

question: The 1996 Eidos game Tomb Raider features a British archaeologist with twin pistols, a long braid, and tank-treads of polygon. Name her.
context: Designed by Toby Gard at Core Design in Derby, England. Angelina Jolie played her in the 2001 film. The original PS1 model had only 540 polygons — most of them on Lara herself.

question: Rare's 1997 N64 split-screen shooter let four players hunt each other through a James Bond film's levels. The hated short-character pick was the bowler-hatted henchman from Goldfinger. Name him.
context: Oddjob's shorter stature meant bullets often passed over his head — friends made house rules banning him. The split-screen four-player mode was added late in development and became the killer feature.

question: Bungie's 2001 Xbox launch shooter Halo: Combat Evolved stars a green-armored super-soldier guided by a blue AI named Cortana. What's the soldier called?
context: Master Chief's full designation is Spartan-117 — but he's only called by it once in the original game. His face is never shown in the trilogy. Voice actor Steve Downes recorded his lines while standing because he felt it sounded more authoritative.

question: In the 1986 NES game Metroid, the player controlled a bounty hunter in an orange power suit. The huge twist — revealed only on a fast finish — was what?
context: Metroid director Yoshio Sakamoto and designer Gunpei Yokoi kept Samus's identity hidden from the marketing and manual. Faster endings revealed more — the under-three-hour ending famously showed her in a bikini, an early-arcade tradition.

question: In Midway's 1992 Mortal Kombat, the announcer yells a specific phrase when an opponent has been beaten and is staggering, prompting the winner to perform a gruesome finishing move. What does he yell?
context: The 'FINISH HIM!' prompt gave the player about five seconds to input the Fatality button-sequence specific to each character. Scorpion's Fatality — ripping off his mask and breathing fire — was the most replicated on schoolyards.

question: Sega's 1989 16-bit console — the platform that launched Sonic and the Mortal Kombat blood code — was called what in North America?
context: Known as the Mega Drive in Japan and Europe. Sega's 'Genesis does what Nintendon't' campaign was a generation-defining piece of console-war marketing. The system was discontinued in 1997.

question: What does NES stand for — the gray-and-black 1985 Nintendo console that came with the Super Mario Bros / Duck Hunt combo cart?
context: Nintendo designed the front-loading cartridge slot to look like a VCR so retailers — burned by the 1983 crash — would shelve it next to home video instead of in the toy aisle.

question: Pac-Man is chased by exactly how many ghosts inside the maze?
context: Blinky (red, direct chase), Pinky (pink, ambush ahead of Pac-Man), Inky (cyan, uses Blinky's position in a complex calc), and Clyde (orange, wanders randomly). Each ghost's personality was deliberate.

question: In the Super Mario Bros series, Mario most often rescues the kingdom's pink-dressed princess from a giant spike-shelled turtle-dragon king. Name the king.
context: Known in Japan as Koopa. The princess he kidnaps was named Princess Toadstool in the US until Super Mario 64 (1996) renamed her Peach. The Bowser-Peach kidnapping plot is the franchise's running joke.

question: A 1983 arcade game presented as a Saturday-morning cartoon — the player nudges the joystick at the right second to make a knight named Dirk dodge dragons and save a princess. What was the game called?
context: Animated by former Disney legend Don Bluth (The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail). The game ran off a laserdisc — the first arcade title to do so. Stranger Things' Dustin Henderson loves it.

question: Sony's 2000 black DVD-playing console — the best-selling home console of all time at over 155 million units — was called what?
context: The PS2's DVD playback was a major selling point — DVD players still cost $300+ in 2000 and the PS2 played them at $299 plus games. Launch lineup included SSX, Tekken Tag, and Madden 2001.

question: Capcom's 1991 Street Fighter II added the first playable female fighter — a Chinese Interpol detective in a blue cheongsam dress with white boots and ox-horn hair. Name her.
context: Designer Akira Yasuda based her costume on Chinese opera. Her signature move is the Hyakuretsukyaku — Hundred Rending Legs — a rapid kick performed by mashing the kick button. Her flip kick (Spinning Bird Kick) is iconic.

question: Namco's 1994 3D arcade fighter featured Jin Kazama, Heihachi, and Yoshimitsu in the long-running Mishima-family feud. What was the series called?
context: Tekken means 'iron fist' in Japanese. Sega's Virtua Fighter (1993) actually beat it to the 3D fighter market, but Tekken's PS1 port made the home transition smoother. The Mishima family feud has been the series' through-line since the original.

question: Seth Gordon's 2007 documentary about Steve Wiebe and Billy Mitchell trading the Donkey Kong world record was called what?
context: Full title: The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters. The film became a cult hit and made household names of obscure arcade-scene figures Walter Day (Twin Galaxies founder), Billy Mitchell (the pizza-parlor owner), and Steve Wiebe (the high-school teacher).

question: Nintendo's 2006 console used a wand-like controller that detected motion — players swung it to hit tennis balls and bowl strikes. Wii Sports came packed in. Name the system.
context: Nintendo intentionally chose 'Wii' — pronounced 'we' — to signal a console for everyone, not just gamers. The blue-ocean strategy worked: Wii sold 101 million units, outselling the technologically superior 360 and PS3.

question: Konami's famous cheat code — entered on the title screen of Contra and dozens of other NES games — begins with how many ups?
context: The full code: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A. In Contra it gave 30 lives. The code was originally created by Konami developer Kazuhisa Hashimoto for the 1986 game Gradius because he found his own game too hard.

question: In Super Mario 64, Mario must collect Power Stars by jumping into magical paintings inside a castle. How many Stars in total can he collect?
context: Only 70 Stars are required to face Bowser in the final battle, but completionists collect all 120 to unlock Yoshi on the roof of the castle. SM64 launched the N64 in June 1996 and redefined 3D platforming.

question: The 1980 Namco arcade hit Pac-Man's iconic round shape came to the designer when he looked at a pizza with one slice missing. Who was the Namco designer?
context: Iwatani also designed the ghost AI: Blinky chases directly, Pinky tries to ambush, Inky uses a complex calc involving Blinky's position, and Clyde wanders randomly. Pac-Man became the first widely-licensed video-game character.

question: In Nintendo's 1981 arcade game Donkey Kong, the player controls a hero originally called Jumpman who climbs scaffolding to rescue a maiden. By the 1982 sequel Donkey Kong Jr., Jumpman had been renamed. What was his new name?
context: Mario was named after Mario Segale, Nintendo of America's warehouse landlord in Tukwila WA, who reportedly stormed into a staff meeting demanding overdue rent. Miyamoto designed Mario's red hat and mustache to work around NES sprite limitations.

question: Atari's 1972 Pong, the first commercial arcade-video hit, was co-developed by an Atari co-founder who later founded Chuck E. Cheese. Name the co-founder.
context: Bushnell tasked engineer Allan Alcorn with building Pong as a training exercise. Alcorn made it too good and it became Atari's first hit. Bushnell sold Atari to Warner in 1976 for $28M and later founded Chuck E. Cheese as a way to put arcade machines in front of kids.

question: Taito's 1978 arcade hit Space Invaders was so popular in Japan that it allegedly caused a national shortage of which physical thing?
context: Designer Tomohiro Nishikado. The story of the 100-yen shortage is partly folklore — coin production did rise in 1978 — but Space Invaders genuinely earned over $2 billion by 1982, making it one of the highest-grossing entertainment products in history.

question: Atari's 1981 arcade hit Centipede was one of the only major arcade titles co-designed by a woman. Name the Atari programmer.
context: Bailey came to Atari from General Motors, where she had written 6502 assembly for embedded car systems. She designed Centipede with Ed Logg, intending the bright pastel colors and arcing screen movement to appeal to a broader audience than the prevailing shoot-em-up boys.

question: Williams Electronics' 1981 arcade hit Defender — famous for its brutally hard, two-joystick-plus-buttons control scheme — was designed by which programmer who would also design Robotron 2084?
context: Jarvis designed Defender to be intentionally hard — the player flies a spacecraft over a horizontal landscape, rescuing humanoids from alien abductors while juggling thrust, fire, and smart bombs. Robotron 2084 (1982) was the dual-stick blueprint that Geometry Wars later popularized.

question: Stern Electronics' 1980 maze-shooter arcade game — one of the first arcade games with synthesized voice ('Got the humanoid! Got the intruder!') — was called what?
context: Designed by Alan McNeil. Berzerk's electronic-voice chip set the player against robots Otto and lookalikes. In 1981, a 19-year-old player at a Calumet City IL arcade died of a heart attack after posting a high score — leading to a parental-panic episode and the 'Berzerk killed a man' urban legend.

question: Atari's 1979 monochrome vector-graphics hit pitted the player's wedge-shaped ship against splitting space rocks. What was the game called?
context: Designed by Ed Logg and Lyle Rains. Players quickly discovered the 'lurking' exploit: clearing all but one small asteroid, then hiding while waiting for UFOs to shoot for high points. Atari later patched it by ramping UFO frequency.

question: Nintendo's 1981 Donkey Kong was originally designed as an adaptation of a syndicated comic strip — until the deal fell through and Nintendo redesigned the characters as Jumpman, Pauline, and DK. Which licensed property?
context: The Popeye license eventually came through and Nintendo released a Popeye arcade in 1982 — but by then DK was already an enormous hit. Designer Miyamoto's first game was DK; he was 28 years old.

question: Konami's 1981 arcade hit — about an amphibian crossing a busy road and a river full of logs and turtles to reach home — was called what?
context: Frogger was distributed in the US by Sega/Gremlin. Its eight-direction joystick (no diagonals) and one-life-at-a-time-on-a-lily-pad design influenced decades of crossing-style games. A Seinfeld 1998 episode 'The Frogger' was built around George trying to move an arcade cabinet across a street.

question: Gottlieb's 1982 arcade hit Q*bert features an orange creature with a tubular nose hopping on an isometric pyramid of cubes. When the player loses a life, Q*bert emits what kind of speech bubble?
choices: A sad face with rolling tears
A red exclamation point in a triangle
context: Designed by Warren Davis and Jeff Lee. The @!#?@! grawlix cloud became a Q*bert signature. Lee also created the iconic sound chip noise Q*bert makes — generated by a coil-spring impact sensor mounted in the cabinet.

question: Namco's 1981 fixed-shooter sequel Galaga improved on its 1979 predecessor by adding a tractor-beam capture mechanic and bonus stages. What was the 1979 predecessor called?
context: Galaxian (1979) introduced the dive-bombing enemy pattern. Galaga added the dual-fighter recovery — letting the captured ship fly alongside the rescued one for double firepower. Galaga famously cameos in Joss Whedon's 2012 Avengers when a SHIELD employee on the helicarrier is caught playing it.

question: Cinematronics' 1983 arcade hit Dragon's Lair ran on a 12-inch LaserDisc and looked like an animated Disney film. Which former Disney animator directed the animation?
context: Bluth had left Disney in 1979 with several colleagues to form Don Bluth Productions. Dragon's Lair cost 50 cents per play — twice the going arcade rate — and earned it back. The hero is Dirk the Daring; the princess is Daphne; the villain is the dragon Singe.

question: Williams Electronics' 1982 arcade hit pits the player on a flying ostrich, mashing the flap button to gain altitude over an opponent on a buzzard for a head-to-head lance joust. Name the game.
context: Designed by John Newcomer. Co-op two-player Joust was the killer two-player arcade experience of the era. Newcomer chose ostriches because the design needed an animal that visually communicated mid-air flapping while still looking heroic.

question: Namco's 1982 arcade game has the player digging through underground tunnels and inflating dragon-like Pookas and fire-breathing Fygars with a pump until they pop. Name the game.
context: Designed by Masahisa Ikegami. The protagonist's real name was Taizo Hori — a Japanese pun on 'horitai zo' meaning 'I want to dig.' Dig Dug's hero went on to become the father of Mr. Driller (1999), a Namco mid-sized franchise of its own.

question: Williams Electronics' 1982 dual-joystick arcade hit pitted the player against waves of attacking robots, with one stick to move and one stick to aim and shoot. Name the Eugene Jarvis title.
context: Jarvis designed Robotron's twin-stick controls after breaking his hand in a car accident — the simpler-than-keyboard scheme was easier for his recovering hand. The control scheme later defined Smash TV (1990), Geometry Wars (2003), and countless indie shooters.

question: Pac-Man's red ghost is the most aggressive — he chases Pac-Man directly along the shortest grid path. What is his name?
context: Iwatani designed each ghost with a distinct AI: Blinky (red) — direct chase; Pinky (pink) — ambush ahead of Pac-Man's facing direction; Inky (cyan) — flanks using a vector from Blinky; Clyde (orange) — wanders randomly when close to Pac-Man. The personalities have been preserved across every port.

question: Sega's 1986 arcade racer let the player drive a Ferrari Testarossa convertible across European-looking branching roads, with selectable in-game radio stations. Who was the Sega arcade designer behind it?
context: Suzuki had also designed Hang-On (1985) and would later design After Burner (1987), Virtua Fighter (1993), Shenmue (1999), and the Virtua series. OutRun's three songs — Magical Sound Shower, Splash Wave, and Passing Breeze — by Hiroshi Kawaguchi defined arcade-driving music.

question: When Mortal Kombat was ported to home consoles in 1993, the Sega Genesis version preserved the arcade blood and fatalities behind a six-button code entered at the title screen. What was the code?
context: The Genesis ABACABB code is a tribute to Genesis (the band) and their 1981 album of the same name. The SNES port lacked blood entirely until Mortal Kombat II (1994). The Genesis port outsold the SNES version, partly because of the code.

question: When Nintendo's NES launched in North America on October 18, 1985, the killer pack-in game that demonstrated what the system could do was what?
context: SMB's World 1-1 has been studied as a masterclass in tutorial design — within 30 seconds the player learns that Goombas hurt you, mushrooms power you up, jumping on enemies is the attack, and that question-blocks dispense items. Designed by Miyamoto with Takashi Tezuka.

question: Super Mario Bros. (1985) contains a famous secret in World 1-2 where the player can run across the top of the level — above the ceiling — to find pipes that warp directly to a later world. What worlds do those three pipes lead to?
context: The other Warp Zone is in World 4-2 and leads to Worlds 5, 6, and 7. The 'minus world' glitch (W -1) is reached by clipping past the warp-zone wall instead of entering it normally — a frame-perfect jump as Mario emerges from a pipe.

question: Sega's 1991 mascot Sonic the Hedgehog was created by a programmer who insisted Sonic move faster than any platformer hero before him. Name him.
context: Designer Naoto Ohshima created Sonic's visual look; programmer Yuji Naka built the rolling-physics engine that made Sonic feel uniquely fast. Sega Technical Institute team (later including Mark Cerny, future PlayStation architect) produced Sonic 2 in 1992.

question: Nintendo's 1986 Famicom Disk System hit — directed by Shigeru Miyamoto, the first NES game with a battery-backed save — let the player explore a top-down overworld with eight numbered labyrinths and a final ninth dungeon. Name the game.
context: Miyamoto credited his childhood exploration of caves and forests near Sonobe, Kyoto, as the inspiration. The gold-colored cartridge of the US release was a Nintendo of America marketing decision to make the box stand out on shelves.

question: Nintendo's 1998 N64 title — directed by Eiji Aonuma and Miyamoto, with Koji Kondo's score — was widely hailed as the best game of its era. Adult Link wields the Master Sword. Name it.
context: Ocarina of Time's Z-targeting (named for the N64's Z trigger) revolutionized 3D-game camera and combat design. The Water Temple — designed by Yoichi Yamada — became the most-cursed dungeon in series history for its iron boots inventory-swapping.

question: When Squaresoft released Final Fantasy VII in 1997, it shipped on a number of CD-ROM discs that astounded players used to single-cartridge games. How many discs?
context: FF7's full data — pre-rendered backgrounds, FMV cutscenes, voice-light audio — wouldn't fit on a 64MB Nintendo 64 cartridge, which is why Square moved to Sony's PlayStation. The move broke the Nintendo-Square partnership and made FF a PlayStation flagship for two decades.

question: Squaresoft's 1995 SNES time-travel JRPG featured character designs by which Dragon Ball mangaka, alongside writing by Sakaguchi and Horii?
context: Chrono Trigger's 'Dream Team' was Hironobu Sakaguchi (Final Fantasy), Yuji Horii (Dragon Quest), and Toriyama (Dragon Ball). Director Takashi Tokita and music by Yasunori Mitsuda (his breakthrough work; he was hospitalized from overwork during the score).

question: Rare's 1997 N64 hit GoldenEye 007 popularized a multiplayer weapon that the player could plant on walls and floors, set to detonate when an enemy approached. What was it called?
context: Designed by Martin Hollis's team at Rare, GoldenEye's multiplayer was added late in development as an experiment. The proximity-mine-only mode — players laying mines and waiting — was a Friday-night campus staple from 1997 through 2001.

question: Capcom's 1996 survival-horror hit on the PlayStation — set in a Spencer Mansion full of zombies and a writhing tongue plant — was directed by which Capcom auteur?
context: Mikami also directed Resident Evil 4 (2005), which fundamentally redefined third-person shooter cinematography with its over-the-shoulder camera. The original RE was famous for its prerendered backgrounds, fixed camera angles, and infamously stilted voice-acting ('Jill sandwich').

question: Konami's 1998 PS1 stealth hit Metal Gear Solid — the first 3D entry in the series, starring Solid Snake — was directed by which Konami auteur whose name became synonymous with cinematic gaming?
context: Kojima had directed Metal Gear (1987) and Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake (1990) for the MSX2 home computer in Japan. MGS1's Psycho Mantis boss famously required the player to physically unplug the controller and re-plug it into Port 2 to defeat his mind-reading.

question: Pokemon Red and Blue (Japan 1996, US 1998) were designed by Game Freak's founder, who based the bug-collecting concept on his childhood hobby of catching bugs in Tokyo creeks. Name him.
context: Tajiri pitched the idea to Nintendo in 1990 — it took six years to ship. Original character art by Ken Sugimori. Composer Junichi Masuda wrote all the original music on a Game Boy with a tracker. The franchise has since become the highest-grossing IP in history.

question: The 1999 Pokemon Trading Card Game Base Set in English was published by Wizards of the Coast — the same company behind Magic: The Gathering. The single most-coveted card in the set is a holographic version of which Pokemon?
context: The Base Set Charizard holo, especially in 'Shadowless' or '1st Edition' subprints, regularly sells for thousands of dollars. The original print run distinguished by a thin shadow border on the right side of the card frame. A PSA 10 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard has sold for over $400,000.

question: Tetris was created in 1984 by a programmer at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. Name him.
context: Pajitnov developed it on an Elektronika 60 — a Soviet-built PDP-11 clone. The game escaped Soviet borders through ELORG (Electronorgtechnica), which licensed it via a labyrinth of disputes resolved by Henk Rogers and Nintendo in 1989, bundling it with the Game Boy.

question: After the 1983 video-game crash, Atari was rumored to have buried millions of unsold cartridges — especially of its disastrous 1982 E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial — in a desert landfill. In what New Mexico city?
context: The story was treated as urban legend until April 26, 2014, when a documentary team led by Zak Penn (writer of Ready Player One) excavated the Alamogordo city landfill and confirmed it — finding thousands of Atari cartridges, console parts, and crushed Atari paperwork.

question: Sega launched its final console — the Dreamcast — in North America on a famous date because of its quirky numerical alignment. What was the date?
context: Sega's 9/9/99 marketing campaign was a huge launch hit — the Dreamcast set first-day-sales records. It launched with NFL 2K, Sonic Adventure, and Soulcalibur. Sega discontinued the console in March 2001 after PS2 dominance crushed it.

question: The composer of the Super Mario Bros overworld theme and the Legend of Zelda main theme — both written for the NES sound chip in 1985-1986 — has been Nintendo's signature composer for forty years. Name him.
context: Kondo joined Nintendo in 1984 as the company's first dedicated music composer. The SMB overworld theme is the most-recognized piece of video-game music ever written. Kondo also scored Star Fox 64, Super Mario 64, and most Zelda main themes.

question: On July 4, 1982, a 17-year-old Florida pizza-parlor owner named Billy Mitchell achieved the first verified score over 1,000,000 points in Donkey Kong. What was his exact score?
context: Mitchell's 874,300 stood as the world record until Steve Wiebe submitted 1,006,600 in 2003. Mitchell countered with a videotaped 1,047,200 in 2007. In 2018, Twin Galaxies disqualified Mitchell's tapes after analysis showed MAME emulator boot-up patterns inconsistent with arcade hardware.

question: Pac-Man's so-called 'kill screen' occurs at the level where the bonus-fruit table integer overflows. The right half of the maze becomes a garbled mess of letters, numbers, and tile-bits that prevents the player from finishing the dot field. What level is the kill screen?
context: 256 is the 8-bit unsigned integer overflow — the level counter wraps around. Billy Mitchell achieved the first publicly verified perfect Pac-Man game in 1999 — every dot, every fruit, every ghost, on every level through 255, ending with a planned death on 256. Score: 3,333,360.

question: Donkey Kong's 'kill screen' occurs at a specific level where the bonus timer initializes too low for Mario to complete the level. Players can climb a single rivet before the timer runs out. What is the level?
context: DK has 117 distinct screens cycling across stages and levels — the kill screen is on the 117th screen, technically the first screen of level 22. The bonus timer is calculated as 0x10 * (level + 1) but with a sign-bit bug at level 22 yielding effectively 0 seconds.

question: Ms. Pac-Man (1982), one of the highest-grossing arcade games in US history, was originally an unauthorized hack of Pac-Man created by Boston students at General Computer Corporation. Midway licensed and rebadged it. What was the unauthorized hack called?
context: GCC's Doug Macrae and Kevin Curran built Crazy Otto as a maze game with leg-having characters. Midway approached them and licensed it as the official Pac-Man sequel, much to Namco's annoyance — Namco hadn't authorized any sequel and only later embraced Ms. Pac-Man as canon in 2002.

question: The world's authoritative arcade-high-score governing body for decades was founded in 1981 by Walter Day in a small Iowa town where Day ran an actual arcade. What town?
context: Day chose Ottumwa because his family owned a hotel there. Twin Galaxies the arcade opened November 1981. Day became a sort of arcade-scene Mr. Rogers, eventually nicknamed 'the referee' for his constant scorebook updates. The 2007 King of Kong documentary made him a household name.

question: Galaga (1981) contains a famous exploit discovered by players: if the player kills all enemies except two specific aliens of a specific color and waits ~15 minutes, the remaining aliens stop firing entirely, allowing the player to safely score forever. What color are those non-firing aliens?
context: The exploit is a bug in Galaga's collision-detection table — Namco's programmers later acknowledged it. Top score-runners exploit it to grind to 999,990 (the score-display rollover) before continuing. The exploit works on the arcade original but was patched in most home ports.

question: An arcade-cabinet urban legend describes a black-cabinet game that allegedly appeared in 1981 Portland Oregon arcades, ran for a few weeks, caused seizures and behavioral changes in players, and was removed by men in black suits. What was the cabinet supposedly named?
context: Polybius first appeared on coinop.org in 1998 as a speculative listing. No evidence supports its existence. The legend is widely treated as the foundational creepypasta of arcade culture, parodied in The Simpsons (S25 'Married to the Blob') with a black cabinet labeled 'PROPERTY OF U.S. GOV'T'.

question: The infamous 1982 Atari 2600 game E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial — often blamed as a major cause of the 1983 video-game crash — was developed in roughly five weeks by a single Atari programmer rushing for a Christmas release. Who?
context: Warshaw had also designed Atari's hit Yars' Revenge (1982). Atari paid $20-25 million for the E.T. license and ordered five million cartridges; only 1.5 million sold. Warshaw still defends the design publicly — it's a complex pit-falling collection game, not 'the worst game ever,' but the rush job and the public memory have stuck.

question: Nintendo launched the Famicom in Japan on July 15, 1983 — two years before the NES reached the US. The launch lineup was three Nintendo arcade ports. What three games?
answer: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye
choices: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye
Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros., and Mario Tennis
Excitebike, Ice Climber, and Balloon Fight
context: The Famicom (Family Computer) was designed by Masayuki Uemura and released for ¥14,800 — about $66 in 1983 USD. The 'NES' redesign for the US was a deliberate VCR-look to avoid the 'toy' aisle still poisoned by the 1983 crash.

question: The Atari 2600 console (released 1977) was originally marketed under a different three-letter acronym; Atari renamed it after introducing the 5200 in 1982. What was the 2600's launch acronym?
context: Atari renamed the VCS to 2600 in 1982 after launching the more advanced 5200. The 2600's joystick had a single button and eight-direction stick. Combat was the pack-in game. Activision was founded in 1979 by Atari programmers angry that Warner Atari wouldn't credit them on cartridges.

question: Super Mario Bros. 2 in North America (1988) was actually a different game from the Japanese sequel. Nintendo of America thought the real SMB2 (later called The Lost Levels) was too hard and reskinned a different Japanese Famicom game for the US market. What was the original game?
context: Doki Doki Panic was a 1987 Famicom Disk System game with mascots from a Fuji TV festival. Nintendo redrew the player-characters as Mario, Luigi, Toad, and Princess Peach. The true Japanese SMB2 finally reached the West in Super Mario All-Stars on SNES (1993) as 'The Lost Levels.'

question: Mattel's 1989 NES peripheral — featured prominently in the 1989 Nintendo-promotional film The Wizard, where the villain calls it 'so bad' — was a glove that read finger movement using infrared. What was it called?
context: The Power Glove worked terribly — only two games used it (Super Glove Ball and Bad Street Brawler), and even those required arduous button-code memorization. Its place in pop-culture is far larger than its actual gaming utility, thanks to The Wizard and reverence in Spielberg's Ready Player One.

question: The Famicom (1983) had two hardwired controllers — Controller 1 with select/start buttons, and Controller 2 with an additional component instead of select/start that Controller 1 lacked. What was the unique component on Controller 2?
context: The Famicom Controller 2 microphone was used in only a few games — most famously The Legend of Zelda, where shouting into the mic killed the Pol's Voice enemy in the eighth dungeon. Western Zelda players had no idea why the enemy was undefeatable — the US NES controller had no mic.

question: Square's 1987 Final Fantasy got its name because creator Hironobu Sakaguchi believed it would be his final game before quitting the industry — Square was nearly bankrupt. Where had Sakaguchi attended college and was planning to return for what graduate degree?
answer: Yokohama National University, for an engineering degree
choices: Yokohama National University, for an engineering degree
Tokyo University, for a literature degree
Kyoto University, for a music degree
Waseda University, for a business degree
context: Sakaguchi was a Yokohama National University engineering student before joining Square. Final Fantasy sold 400,000 copies in Japan, saving the company. Sakaguchi went on to direct Final Fantasy through VI, executive-produce VII-IX, and create Chrono Trigger with Yuji Horii and Akira Toriyama.

question: Sega's 1998 Dreamcast launch title in Japan and 1999 US launch — the first fully 3D Sonic game — was produced by which Sonic Team founder who had also directed Nights into Dreams (1996)?
context: Sonic Adventure introduced new characters Big the Cat (fishing), Tails (mech), Knuckles (treasure-hunting), Amy Rose (escape), and E-102 Gamma (shooter) — each with their own gameplay style. The 'Crush 40' rock-vocal tracks by Jun Senoue became signature Sonic-3D-era music. Sonic Team's Takashi Iizuka also co-directed.

question: In Rare's GoldenEye 007 (1997), the most coveted multiplayer weapon could kill any opponent with a single shot. It also held only a small number of bullets at a time. What's it called?
context: Based on the Scaramanga golden pistol from the 1974 Bond film. Holds one bullet; one-shot kills anything. Spawned in random multiplayer locations, leading to mad scrambles. Many multiplayer house-rules tournaments forbid camping the Golden Gun spawn — and forbid Oddjob entirely.

question: In Metal Gear Solid (1998), the boss Psycho Mantis appears to read the player's mind by dodging every attack. Veteran players solved the puzzle by interacting with the PS1 hardware in an unusual way. What did the player have to do?
answer: Move the controller from Port 1 to Port 2
choices: Move the controller from Port 1 to Port 2
Hold the dualshock motion sensors face-down
Insert a memory card into Slot 2 mid-fight
Press Start while the disc tray was open
context: Psycho Mantis 'read your mind' by reading controller inputs from Port 1 — switching ports cut him off. Earlier in the fight, he also reads the player's memory card and comments on other Konami games saved there ('I see you also like Castlevania!'). Kojima's fourth-wall-breaking signature.

question: Super Mario Bros: The Lost Levels — the original Japanese SMB2 — first reached North America in a 1993 SNES compilation that also included enhanced 16-bit remakes of SMB1, SMB2 (US), and SMB3. What was the compilation called?
context: All-Stars rebuilt all four NES games with 16-bit graphics by Nintendo R&D4. The Lost Levels added poison mushrooms, wind, and brutal difficulty. The cartridge also came in a Mario World pack-in version. The 1996 Super Mario All-Stars + Super Mario World combined edition is one of the rarest SNES carts.

question: The Sega Dreamcast (1998-2001) controller had a slot for a small memory card with its own LCD screen, D-pad, and buttons — it could be detached and played as a tiny standalone Tamagotchi-like device. What was the card called?
context: The VMU had 200 blocks of memory and a 48x32 LCD. Sonic Adventure's 'Chao Garden' could be loaded onto the VMU and raised standalone. Sony's PlayStation 1 PocketStation (1999, Japan-only) had a similar concept. The Sega VMU defines a forgotten era of console-peripheral creativity.

question: The Super Nintendo launched in North America on August 23, 1991, with a single pack-in cartridge. What was the pack-in launch title?
context: Super Mario World was developed by Miyamoto's team alongside the SNES hardware itself, debuting Yoshi the dinosaur. The launch lineup also included F-Zero, Pilotwings, SimCity, and Gradius III. Nintendo had been beaten to 16-bit in the US by Sega Genesis (1989), but the SNES caught up by 1993.

question: Chrono Trigger's 1995 SNES score was composed by a then-25-year-old Squaresoft programmer who was so determined to compose a score that he threatened to quit if not given the chance. He was hospitalized from overwork during the composition. Name him.
context: Nobuo Uematsu — Square's main composer — stepped in to write 10 of the game's 65 tracks when Mitsuda fell ill. Mitsuda went on to score Xenogears (1998) and Chrono Cross (1999). His 'Corridors of Time' and 'Schala's Theme' are considered among the best JRPG compositions ever.

question: Sega released Sonic 3 (1994) and Sonic & Knuckles (1994) for the Genesis as two cartridges sold separately. The S&K cartridge had a passthrough slot on top, allowing the player to plug Sonic 3 into S&K and play them as a single combined game. What was that combined experience called?
context: Plugging Sonic 2 into the S&K cartridge let the player play as Knuckles in Sonic 2 (no extra story). Plugging Sonic 1 or any non-Sonic cart yielded the 'No Way' or 'Blue Sphere' randomly generated minigame. The lock-on cartridge tech was an engineering one-off — Sega never used it again.

question: In the original 1992 Mortal Kombat arcade, a secret green ninja character appeared on the Pit stage and could be fought after meeting specific conditions. The character had no playable selection in MK1 but was added as playable in MK2. What was the green ninja's name?
context: MK1's secret-character lore — silhouettes flying across the moon, double-flawless rounds, no-block challenges — was a closely-guarded arcade rumor. Reptile's combination of Scorpion's spear and Sub-Zero's freeze made him a fan-favorite. MK2 added Smoke, Noob Saibot, and Jade as similar secret-ninja characters.

question: In Capcom's 1994 Super Street Fighter II Turbo, a hidden boss could be challenged by meeting specific arcade conditions. This corrupted dark-energy ninja master is a brother to Ryu and Ken's sensei Gouken. What's the hidden boss called?
context: Akuma's name means 'devil' in Japanese — Capcom renamed him for the US to avoid licensing conflicts with Mike Tyson's then-promoter, similar to how Vega/Bison/Balrog were renamed in a three-way swap. Akuma's signature finisher Shun Goku Satsu (Raging Demon) was the first SF combo with cinematic camerawork.

question: Konami's 1998 Japan-arcade hit Dance Dance Revolution introduced an entirely new genre — rhythm games with foot-pad controllers. DDR was part of a broader Konami brand that included Beatmania (1997) and Guitar Freaks (1999). What was the brand called?
context: Bemani is short for 'Beat Mania.' DDR reached the US in 1999 and exploded among gym-class fitness programs by the early 2000s. The game's combination of public-arcade visibility, calorie burn, and music-discovery appeal made it the rare rhythm game to cross into mass-culture awareness.

question: Sega released a Genesis add-on in 1994 that plugged into the Genesis cartridge slot to add 32-bit processing power. The product was rushed to market alongside the upcoming Sega Saturn and was discontinued within a year. What was it called?
context: The 32X had its own power supply, AV cables, and required the Genesis to function — a mushroom-tower of plastic. Only 40-ish games were ever released for it, including Doom (with weaker graphics than 3DO), Star Wars Arcade, and Virtua Racing Deluxe. The Sega Saturn launch six months later cannibalized 32X sales.

question: The Nintendo 64 controller (1996) had an unusual three-pronged design — left grip with D-pad, center grip with analog stick, right grip with face buttons. The player chose two of three grips to hold. What was the central component that defined which two grips?
context: The N64 analog stick was the first analog stick on a major home console — Sony quickly responded with the DualShock (1997). Holding left+center vs left+right depended on what the game needed; Super Mario 64 used center+right, while Mario Party gripped left+right for D-pad-heavy mini-games.

question: Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) features Master Chief's AI companion Cortana, voiced by an actress who would continue voicing her through Halo 5. The actress was a regular on the TV series Firefly. Name her.
context: Wait — that's wrong; she wasn't on Firefly. Jen Taylor was on the radio adaptation Lost Universe, but Firefly's named cast was different. Taylor also voiced Princess Peach in Mario Kart 64 (1996) and was Microsoft's voice of Cortana the assistant. Steve Downes voices Master Chief.

question: Crash Bandicoot (1996) was the first big PlayStation hit from Naughty Dog. The studio was co-founded in 1986 by two University of Michigan classmates. Name the co-founders.
choices: Mark Cerny and Naughty Dog Anonymous
context: Gavin and Rubin's earlier games included Keef the Thief (1989), Rings of Power (1991), and Way of the Warrior (1994). After Crash, they made Jak and Daxter for PS2, sold Naughty Dog to Sony in 2001, and left in 2004. The studio went on to make Uncharted (Amy Hennig) and The Last of Us (Neil Druckmann).

question: Resident Evil 4 (2005, GameCube) shifted the franchise camera from fixed-angle pre-rendered backgrounds to an over-the-shoulder third-person perspective. The change reinvented action-game cinematography. What was the in-fiction setting?
context: Leon S. Kennedy travels to rural Spain to rescue the US President's kidnapped daughter Ashley from a parasite-cult called Los Iluminados. Director Shinji Mikami's over-the-shoulder camera was directly imitated by Gears of War (2006), Uncharted (2007), and Dead Space (2008), defining the post-2005 action-shooter look.

question: Midway's 1993 arcade hit NBA Jam featured 2-on-2 basketball with absurd dunking and a famous announcer who would shout 'HE'S ON FIRE!' when a player made three baskets in a row. Who was the announcer?
context: Kitzrow's catchphrases — 'Boomshakalaka!', 'From way downtown!', 'He's heating up!' — were largely improvised in a single Chicago recording session. Kitzrow has voiced almost every Midway and NBA Jam-derivative sports title since. He has no formal sports-broadcast career outside game development.

question: Konami's 1991 four-player Simpsons Arcade let players take turns as Homer (punch), Marge (vacuum cleaner), Bart (skateboard), and Lisa (skipping rope) beating up Springfield criminals. Where does the hidden one-up donut famously appear?
answer: Behind the bowling alley garbage cans
choices: Behind the bowling alley garbage cans
Inside the Power Plant cooling tower
On top of the Krusty Burger sign
Down a manhole at the courthouse
context: The Simpsons Arcade is a brawler in the X-Men Arcade / TMNT Arcade tradition — Konami's beat-em-up template. The Bonus Round between stages is the bouncing-on-a-trampoline minigame. Homer's nightmare cutscene featuring a giant donut is one of the more surreal arcade interstitials of the era.

question: Konami's 1989 four-player Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles arcade game let four players each pick a different colored turtle. Which turtle wore the purple mask?
context: Leonardo (blue) wielded katanas. Donatello (purple) wielded a bo staff. Raphael (red) wielded sai. Michelangelo (orange) wielded nunchaku. The Konami arcade is the second TMNT game (after the 1989 NES original), and is widely considered the definitive beat-em-up of the franchise.

question: Disney's 2012 animated film Wreck-It Ralph features cameos from many real video-game characters inside arcade machines. One famous group-therapy scene shows real bad guys meeting — including a Pac-Man enemy chairing the meeting. Which ghost is the chair?
context: Other real-game cameos: Bowser (Mario), M. Bison and Zangief (Street Fighter), Kano (Mortal Kombat), Doctor Robotnik (Sonic), and Neff (Altered Beast). Sonic himself appears with a 'Public Service Announcement' cameo at Game Central Station. Voice direction by John C. Reilly as Ralph.

question: The 1984 sci-fi film The Last Starfighter has a teenage hero recruited by aliens after he beats the high score on an arcade game called Starfighter. The film featured one of the earliest extensive uses of CGI for live-action sequences. What computer rendered the CGI?
context: The Cray X-MP at Digital Productions in Los Angeles rendered the Gunstar spaceship and most space sequences. The film grossed only $28M but became a cult classic. It spawned no sequel but heavily influenced Ready Player One (Ernest Cline cited it as a primary inspiration).

question: Stranger Things Season 2 (2017) features Dustin Henderson trying to get the high score on the Dragon's Lair cabinet at Hawkins' Palace Arcade. Who beats him to the score, becoming the Season 2 'King of Arcade'?
context: Max's MADMAX initials on the leaderboard intrigue the boys for episodes before they meet her. Stranger Things' arcade scenes were filmed at a real reproduction arcade in Atlanta, featuring period-accurate cabinets including Pac-Man, Dragon's Lair, Centipede, and Dig Dug.

question: The 1989 Fred Savage film The Wizard — a feature-length Nintendo commercial about a cross-country video-game tournament — climaxes at Universal Studios Hollywood with the first North American gameplay reveal of which then-unreleased Nintendo title?
context: SMB3 wouldn't release in the US until February 1990. The Wizard's climax shows protagonist Jimmy collecting Warp Whistles in World 1 and warping to World 4. The film promoted the Power Glove and Nintendo Power magazine. Universal sued Nintendo over the use of their Hollywood backlot but eventually settled.

question: On a now-disputed date in 1982 from his Fort Lauderdale FL pizza-parlor home base, Billy Mitchell submitted to Twin Galaxies founder Walter Day the first publicly-verified Donkey Kong score over a million. The tape was sent by courier without public play. For 21 years, no one beat the record. In 2003, Steve Wiebe (a Boeing engineer and Washington high-school teacher) submitted 1,006,600 from his garage cabinet. Mitchell responded with a videotape sent again by courier. What was Mitchell's 2007 response score?
context: The 2007 Seth Gordon documentary The King of Kong tracked the rivalry. Wiebe later beat 1,049,100 publicly. In April 2018, Twin Galaxies analyzed Mitchell's pre-2007 tapes and concluded they had been recorded from MAME emulator rather than arcade hardware — disqualifying all of Mitchell's DK records. The disqualification lawsuit continues.

question: In 2003, Steve Wiebe, a Washington high-school science teacher and recently-laid-off Boeing engineer, built a Donkey Kong cabinet from a damaged board he had bought for $50 on eBay. He set it up in his garage in Redmond WA. His first videotape submission to Twin Galaxies was rejected by referees. What did they question?
answer: The plausibility of his rapid-rivet sequence on the final screen
choices: The plausibility of his rapid-rivet sequence on the final screen
Whether he had used save-state cheats on a board hack
Whether his tape ran over the documented five-hour rules limit
Whether Mitchell had intercepted and substituted the footage
context: In King of Kong, Walter Day sends Twin Galaxies referee Robert Mruczek to inspect Wiebe's cabinet. Mruczek later denied Mitchell or his allies tampered with the inspection; the documentary's villain framing has been disputed by Mitchell's defenders. Wiebe's son Derek and daughter Cannon both appear in the film as kids.

question: The North American video-game industry collapse of 1983-1985 was caused by a combination of saturated console market, low-quality third-party games, and the unsold-cartridge backlog of Atari's two biggest disasters. The two disasters were Atari's 1982 E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial port and which other 1982 Atari title — the licensed port of the most successful arcade game in history?
context: Atari produced 12 million Pac-Man cartridges for a 10-million-installed-base 2600 — they expected to sell to new console buyers. The port's flickering ghosts (a 4-frame palette swap) made it look terrible. Atari sold only 7 million, leaving warehouses full. Combined with E.T., Atari laid off thousands of employees in 1983 and the entire toy aisle stopped stocking games by 1984.

question: Activision was founded in 1979 by four Atari programmers (David Crane of Pitfall!, Larry Kaplan, Alan Miller, and Bob Whitehead) who left after Warner Atari refused to credit designers on cartridge boxes. What was the famous Atari executive comment that triggered their resignation?
answer: That they were no more important to Atari than the assembly-line workers who boxed the cartridges
choices: That they were no more important to Atari than the assembly-line workers who boxed the cartridges
That Bushnell would refuse to honor their stock-option vesting after resignation
That Atari lawyers would sue them for trade-secret breach if they discussed designs
That Kaplan would be fired for putting his name on the title screen of a game
context: Crane and the others split off and immediately released Boxing, Tennis, Skiing, and Dragster. Activision became one of the biggest third-party publishers. Atari sued Activision, but in 1983 settled by allowing third-party publishers — opening the floodgates that contributed to the 1983 crash via low-quality shovelware.

question: Don Bluth Productions was founded in September 1979 when Bluth and 11 colleagues walked out of Disney Animation Studios. Their first film was The Secret of NIMH (1982). Bluth's animation studio later defined the arcade-game-as-cartoon look with Dragon's Lair (1983) and Space Ace (1984). What Disney film were Bluth and team working on at the moment of their walkout?
context: Bluth's 1982 NIMH won the Academy of Science Fiction prize. Steven Spielberg recruited Bluth to direct An American Tail (1986) and The Land Before Time (1988), both major hits. Bluth's 1989 All Dogs Go to Heaven failed against The Little Mermaid (released the same week). The animator's walk-out is widely credited as forcing Disney's late-1980s renaissance under Katzenberg.

question: Sega's CEO Tom Kalinske shocked the industry at E3 May 11, 1995 by announcing the Sega Saturn would launch in North America that same day, earlier than the originally announced September 2 date. The launch backfired badly. Sony immediately countered. What price did Sony announce that day for the PlayStation?
context: Sony's '299' announcement at E3 was the legendary mic-drop moment — Olaf Olafsson of Sony just walked out, said '$299', and left. The Saturn was $399 with only six launch titles. Major retailers KB Toys and Walmart pulled out angrily over being skipped. The Saturn never recovered; Sega exited console hardware after Dreamcast 2001.

question: The PlayStation brand originated as a Nintendo-Sony joint project — Sony was contracted to build a CD-ROM peripheral for the SNES called the 'Play Station.' At Consumer Electronics Show 1991, Sony announced the partnership publicly. The next day, Nintendo announced it was switching CD partners. Who did Nintendo switch to?
choices: Hitachi, which made the Saturn co-processor
context: Nintendo had grown wary of Sony's contract terms — Sony would have kept all the revenue from CD-based games. Switching to Philips humiliated Sony's CES booth team. Ken Kutaragi convinced Sony chairman Norio Ohga to go ahead with the project as a standalone Sony console — the PlayStation. The Philips CD-i went on to be famously disastrous.

question: Bungie Studios was a Macintosh-only game developer in Chicago when Microsoft acquired them in June 2000, partly to secure their unannounced flagship third-person sci-fi shooter as an Xbox launch title. The game was reworked into first-person and renamed. What was the studio's earlier Mac shooter trilogy that established their FPS bona fides?
context: Marathon — Marathon 2: Durandal — Marathon Infinity. Halo was originally a Mac-and-PC RTS, then a third-person shooter, then the FPS Xbox launch we know. Bungie left Microsoft in 2007 to make Destiny under Activision. The Marathon trilogy was open-sourced in 2005 by Bungie.

question: Master Chief's John-117 designation refers to him being the 117th Spartan-II inducted into the program — kidnapped as a six-year-old child in 2517 and replaced by a clone. The Spartan-II project was led by a Halsey-named researcher who appears in the games. What was her first name?
choices: Cortana (the AI is a digital copy)
context: Cortana was created from a flash-cloned copy of Halsey's brain — making her effectively Master Chief's surrogate mother in genetic terms. The Spartan-II program took 75 children; 33 survived augmentation. The Halo: First Strike novel by Eric Nylund (2003) is the canonical Halsey/Chief backstory.

question: Super Mario Bros (1985) was co-designed by Miyamoto and which other Nintendo designer who would become a constant Miyamoto collaborator across Zelda, Mario, and Yoshi titles for 40 years?
context: Tezuka has co-directed almost every major Mario title (he was the producer on Super Mario Maker and Super Mario Wonder). His and Miyamoto's design philosophy — 'design the player's first 30 seconds perfectly' — defines the SMB World 1-1 tutorial, widely studied in game-design programs.

question: In Super Mario Bros World 1-1, the first Goomba appears exactly as Mario moves forward enough to see the first question-mark block. Miyamoto and Tezuka deliberately designed this opening to teach the player a specific lesson via the Goomba's collision. What lesson?
answer: That Goombas hurt on touch and die from jumps
choices: That Goombas hurt on touch and die from jumps
That power-up mushrooms grow Mario bigger
That Mario can break bricks from below
That coins are collected by touching them
context: The 30-second sequence — first Goomba, first question-block with a mushroom that the new player likely runs into, first second-level pipes — was deliberately designed as a no-text tutorial. Designer Mark Brown's 'Sequelitis' YouTube video makes the SMB 1-1 case canonical in modern design analysis.

question: Yoshi first appeared in Super Mario World (1990, SNES launch title), but Miyamoto had wanted a dinosaur mountable companion as far back as the original Super Mario Bros (1985) — the NES hardware couldn't render it. What was Yoshi's original Japanese name on his early concept-sheet?
context: Yoshi's full name was almost never used in-game. The Mario World manual lists him as 'T. Yoshisaur Munchakoopas' in the US release. Designer Shigefumi Hino. Yoshi has appeared in over 30 Mario titles, has his own series (Yoshi's Island 1995, Yoshi's Story 1997, Yoshi's Crafted World 2019), and is Nintendo's third-most-marketable character behind Mario and Pokemon.

question: The NES/Famicom and Game Boy were primarily designed by Nintendo's Research and Development 1 team, led by an engineer who had also created the Game & Watch handheld and the D-pad. What was his name?
context: Yokoi's 'lateral thinking with withered technology' philosophy — using mature, cheap components creatively — produced the Game Boy and the entire Game & Watch line. He left Nintendo in 1996 after the Virtual Boy commercial failure and died in a car accident in October 1997, age 56.

question: Final Fantasy VII (1997 PS1) was the franchise's global breakthrough — selling 9.8 million copies and putting Square at the top of the JRPG world. The game's protagonist Cloud Strife was once a member of Shinra's elite soldier program. What was the program called?
context: SOLDIER is always written in all-caps in-game. SOLDIER 1st Class is the highest rank; Sephiroth was a 1st Class member. Cloud's actual rank history is one of the game's mysteries — explained more fully in Final Fantasy VII Remake (2020-2024) and the Compilation of FFVII (Crisis Core, Advent Children, Dirge of Cerberus).

question: Final Fantasy VII (1997) introduced the Materia system — colored orbs slotted into weapons and armor. Magic Materia was green. Command Materia was yellow. Support Materia was blue. What color was Summon Materia (Ifrit, Shiva, Bahamut)?
context: Five Materia categories: Green (Magic — Fire, Cure, Bolt), Yellow (Command — Steal, Throw, Sense), Blue (Support — All, Quadra Magic, MP Turbo, slotted as a pair), Purple (Independent — passive stat boost), and Red (Summon — Ifrit, Shiva, Bahamut). The system encouraged build experimentation rare for the era.

question: The Nintendo 64 launched in North America on September 29, 1996, over a year and a half after the PlayStation. Nintendo's launch marketing campaign emphasized one specific technical-spec advantage over the 32-bit PlayStation and Saturn. What advantage?
answer: 64-bit CPU processing, twice the bus width of competitors
choices: 64-bit CPU processing, twice the bus width of competitors
CD-quality redbook-audio Game Pak music streams in mono
An on-cart MIDI synthesis chip generating 96 vocal voices
The Z-button trigger as an industry-first analog rear control
context: The N64's 64-bit MIPS R4300i CPU was technically true but marketing-misleading — the actual bus was rarely fully utilized. The launch lineup of two games (Mario 64 and Pilotwings 64) was infamously thin. Nintendo's choice of cartridge over CD-ROM cost them the goodwill of third-party publishers including Square, who took FFVII to PlayStation.

question: Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) ends with an iconic vehicle-driving sequence where Master Chief must escape the exploding Pillar of Autumn ship by driving the M12 Warthog up a ramp through corridors filled with enemy Flood. What is this final vehicle-mission level called?
context: The Maw is the tenth and final level. Bungie designer Jaime Griesemer designed the escape sequence in 12 days at the end of development. The Warthog's physics — a four-wheeled jeep that could be driven over corpses, ramps, and walls — defined the open-arena Halo combat. The escape was so popular that Halo 3 ended with a Warthog escape mirroring it.

question: The Sega Dreamcast (1998-2001) was the first console with a built-in modem — a 33.6k or 56k card included in every unit. Sega's North American online service was called what?
context: SegaNet enabled the first console MMO — Phantasy Star Online (2000), which let players from Japan, US, and Europe play together on shared servers. Dreamarena was the European service. Online play also distinguished NFL 2K1, Quake III Arena Dreamcast, and Chu Chu Rocket. Sega shut down its first-party Dreamcast servers in 2003.

question: The Pokemon Trading Card Game's 1999 English Base Set Charizard holo card came in several printing variants of decreasing rarity. Which one variant — distinguishable by a thin shadow border on the right side of the card art — is the most valuable today?
context: The Base Set's first print run was 'Shadowless' — no thin shadow border was added until the second print. The 'Edition 1' stamp was on the leftmost cards of the first run. A PSA 10 graded 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard has sold for over $400,000 at auction. WotC's Pokemon TCG printing was managed by Carta Mundi in Belgium.

question: Sega's 1991 Genesis brawler Streets of Rage featured a now-legendary soundtrack of house, techno, and electronic dance music by a composer who had earlier scored Revenge of Shinobi (1989) and ActRaiser (1990). Name him.
context: Koshiro was 24 when he scored Streets of Rage. His Streets of Rage 2 score is widely considered the greatest 16-bit OST. He used a custom Atari ST-based MIDI-tracker tool to push the Genesis FM synthesis hardware further than most thought possible. Koshiro continues composing today — Etrian dungeon-crawlers, 7th Dragon, and modern Streets of Rage 4 (2020).

question: Final Fantasy VII's final boss theme 'One-Winged Angel' was Nobuo Uematsu's first piece of orchestral video-game music. He has cited a specific composer's classical influences for the chorus arrangement. What composer specifically?
context: The 'estuans interius' Latin chorus directly echoes Carmina Burana. Uematsu also cites Stravinsky and Jimi Hendrix as influences. Uematsu composed over 100 FF songs from 1987-2003, became Square's de-facto musical face, and now leads his own rock band 'The Black Mages,' which performs orchestral-rock arrangements of his game compositions.

question: Konami's 1999 Silent Hill — created by the Team Silent group at Konami Tokyo — featured a profoundly unsettling industrial-ambient soundtrack composed by which then-30-year-old Konami sound designer?
context: Yamaoka used metal drums, factory machinery, scraping metal, and distorted electronic beats to create the Silent Hill sound. He has scored Silent Hill 1 through Silent Hill: Shattered Memories (2009) and Silent Hill f (2025). The town's foggy, alternate-dimension Otherworld with its rusted iron and bleeding walls was inspired by the films Jacob's Ladder and Eraserhead.

question: GoldenEye 007 (1997, N64) was developed by a small Rare team led by Martin Hollis. The team had no prior FPS experience and developed the multiplayer mode in the final six months of a four-year project. How many people were on the GoldenEye development team?
answer: Nine, including Hollis as project director
choices: Nine, including Hollis as project director
Seventy, the entire Rare studio at the time
context: The nine: Martin Hollis (lead), David Doak (mission designer), Steve Ellis (programmer), Karl Hilton (level artist), Mark Edmonds (programmer), Brett Jones (modeler), Duncan Botwood (level designer), Adrian Smith (modeler), and Graeme Norgate / Grant Kirkhope (music). Multiple team members later founded Free Radical Design and made TimeSplitters (2000).

question: The PlayStation hardware architect was a Sony engineer who had previously developed the SPC700 audio chip used in the SNES. After the Nintendo-Sony partnership fell through in 1991, he convinced Sony to make their own console. Name him.
context: Kutaragi was widely called 'the father of the PlayStation.' He led hardware development for PS1, PS2, PS3, and the early PSP. Sony forced him into retirement in 2007 after PS3's troubled launch. His Cell Broadband Engine processor in the PS3 was simultaneously a research achievement and a developer pain-point that hurt PS3's third-party support.

question: Earthworm Jim (1994, Genesis and SNES) was a bizarre platformer about a worm in a robotic suit. The character was created by a then-young animator who would later create Catscratch and Veggie Tales. Name him.
context: TenNapel sold Earthworm Jim to David Perry's Shiny Entertainment. Perry's team — Nick Bruty, Tom Tanaka, Tommy Tallarico (music) — finished the design. Tallarico's score is considered a high-water mark of Genesis FM synthesis. TenNapel later created Neverhood (1996) on PlayStation, with stop-motion claymation and Terry S Taylor music.

question: Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot (1996) was originally going to be called 'Willie the Wombat,' but the team rejected the name due to a potential trademark conflict. Animator Charles Zembillas and visual designer Joe Pearson designed Crash with what classic American animation studio's house style as a reference?
answer: Looney Tunes (specifically Tex Avery's exaggerated takes)
choices: Looney Tunes (specifically Tex Avery's exaggerated takes)
context: Crash's hyper-exaggerated facial expressions, eyebrow waggles, and head-snap reactions were directly inspired by Avery's wartime cartoons (Red Hot Riding Hood). Pearson and Zembillas had both come from television-cartoon backgrounds. Crash 1's 'Sony Sucks' Bandicoot Mascot Wars marketing campaign was Sony of America's deliberate jab at Sega and Nintendo.

question: When Twin Galaxies disqualified Billy Mitchell's Donkey Kong scores in April 2018, the organization had been sold by Walter Day to a new owner. The current Twin Galaxies' CEO led the technical investigation that confirmed Mitchell's tapes were MAME-emulator captures. Name him.
context: Jace Hall is a Hollywood producer, founder of Monolith Productions (No One Lives Forever, F.E.A.R.), and Twin Galaxies' owner from 2014. The Mitchell investigation used reverse-engineering of arcade-board level-load patterns vs MAME's level-load patterns — a frame-by-frame signature analysis the original Twin Galaxies referees couldn't have done in 2003.

question: The first known video-game Easter egg — a hidden credit reading 'Created by Warren Robinett' — was buried in an Atari 2600 game in 1979 after Atari refused to credit designers on cartridges. The game was an adventure puzzler with a small square hero, three castles, and a dragon. What was the game called?
context: Robinett's hidden credit was placed in the Black Castle, accessible by carrying a pixel-thin 'gray dot' across multiple screens to a specific spot. Atari executives at first wanted Robinett fired for the secret, then realized players loved discovering it. The term 'Easter egg' was coined by Atari Director of Software Steve Wright in 1980 to describe the phenomenon.

question: Atari's 1982 hit Yars' Revenge — a vertical shooter with a fly-like protagonist Yar battling the Qotile cannon behind a force-field — was Howard Scott Warshaw's first big hit, predating his E.T. disaster. The game contained a famous central scrolling band of random colors and pixels called what?
context: The Neutral Zone was a randomly-painted strip of memory bytes — Warshaw used the game's ROM itself as the visual texture. The Yar character was a yellow eight-legged fly-creature; the Qotile alternated between a stationary cannon and a swirly killing-projectile called the Swirl. Yars' Revenge sold over a million copies for the 2600, an enormous hit for the era.

question: NBA Jam Tournament Edition (1994) added hidden non-NBA player characters unlocked by entering specific dates and initials at the title screen. Among the hidden players were US presidential candidates, sitcom characters, and the development team. Which sitting US president appeared as a hidden character?
context: NBA Jam TE's hidden characters: Bill Clinton, Al Gore, Tipper Gore, the Beastie Boys, Frank Thomas, Tonya Harding, several Mortal Kombat fighters, and the entire Midway development team. The Mortal Kombat unlocks featured stretchy-arm versions of Sub-Zero, Scorpion, and Raiden. Many cheat codes were leaked in Electronic Gaming Monthly print articles.

question: The NES was powered by a Ricoh-built variant of which 8-bit CPU — the same CPU family also used in the Apple II, the Commodore 64, and the Atari 2600?
context: The 6502 was designed by Chuck Peddle's team at MOS Technology in 1975 — explicitly to compete with Motorola's 6800 at one-fifth the price. The 6502 dominated 8-bit personal computing of the late 1970s and the entire NES era. Steve Wozniak picked the 6502 for the Apple I (1976) because it was the cheapest CPU he could find — $25 vs the 8080's $359.

question: The first US release of The Legend of Zelda (August 22, 1987) came in a gold-colored cartridge — Nintendo's marketing decision to distinguish it from the standard gray NES carts. The same gold treatment was applied to which 1988 NES sequel?
answer: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
choices: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
Metroid II: Samus Returns Game Boy
Kid Icarus II: Of Myths and Monsters
context: Zelda II is the only other NES game in the gold-cart treatment. The Famicom Disk System Japanese version of Zelda used a literal floppy disk in a yellow-and-blue plastic case. The Disk System's audio expansion chip allowed Koji Kondo to use FM synthesis in the original Zelda — capability the NES motherboard lacked.

question: The Sega Genesis (1989) was powered by what 16-bit CPU — the same CPU family powering the Apple Macintosh, the Atari ST, the Commodore Amiga, and most arcade hardware of the era?
context: The Genesis ran the 68000 at 7.6 MHz with a secondary Zilog Z80 handling audio (a leftover from the Sega Master System architecture). The SNES used the 65816 (a 16-bit 6502 successor) at 3.58 MHz — slower clock but more efficient. 'Blast Processing' was Sega's marketing for the Genesis's faster clock advantage.

question: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 (1992) released globally on Tuesday November 24, 1992 — a marketing event Sega dubbed 'Sonic 2sday.' The game's pack-in introduced a two-tailed fox sidekick. What's his real name (vs. the better-known nickname)?
context: 'Tails' is his nickname. The 'Miles Prower' = 'miles per hour' pun is a Sonic-canon-trivia gem. Tails was designed by Yasushi Yamaguchi at Sega Technical Institute. Sonic 2 was the first major game co-developed between Sega of Japan and Sega Technical Institute (Mark Cerny's team), pioneering the trans-Pacific Sega development pipeline.

question: OutRun (1986) was designed by Yu Suzuki as Sega's signature arcade racer. The game's gimmick was branching road choices at the end of each stage — letting the player pick a left or right path. What kind of cabinet hardware made the racing immersive beyond visuals?
answer: A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car
choices: A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car
Force-feedback in the steering wheel and accelerator pedal
A 3D stereoscopic LCD shutter set for a glassless 3D effect
Wraparound surround-sound speakers in the bucket headrest
context: Suzuki's 'taikan' (full-body) cabinets defined Sega arcade hardware. After Burner (1987) had a yoke that simulated jet roll. Hang-On (1985) had a motorcycle the player straddled. The OutRun cabinet's bright-red convertible Ferrari shape became an arcade icon — the deluxe version is the holy grail of arcade collectors.

question: Konami's 1997 PS1 hit Castlevania: Symphony of the Night was the franchise's pivot from linear levels to open-castle exploration. The game's protagonist was the half-vampire son of Dracula, with a name that's Dracula spelled backwards. What's his name?
context: Alucard's first Castlevania appearance was Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse (1989). Director Koji Igarashi led Symphony of the Night and made it the prototype for the term 'Metroidvania' — open exploration of a castle with item-gated traversal. Original cover art by Ayami Kojima. The opening boss fight with Dracula uses dialogue lifted directly from the SNES Dracula X intro.

question: The original 1985 NES Super Mario Bros contains a glitch in World 1-2 that lets the player enter a strange underwater level with no exit. To trigger it, the player must jump up under a specific pipe with frame-perfect timing to clip past the Warp Zone trigger. The result places Mario in a corrupted level the inventory display labels with a non-numeric tile. What did fans nickname this level?
context: The corrupted tile is interpreted by the game's level-loader as the never-finishing World 7-2 water level — Mario can swim forever but the flagpole never appears. On the Japanese Famicom Disk System, the Minus World corrupts to three different underwater glitch-worlds depending on Mario's exact clip position.

question: The opening scene of Rob Reiner's 1987 The Princess Bride shows a young Fred Savage in bed playing a baseball video game on a Commodore Amiga personal computer while his grandfather (Peter Falk) arrives to read him a story. Production designer Norman Reynolds picked a then-current 1987 sports release from Accolade software. Name the game shown.
context: The Amiga 1000 (released 1985) was the visible hardware in the prop shot. Goldman wrote both the novel and screenplay. Reiner's daughter Tracy famously coined the practical-effects rats in the fire-swamp scene 'pretend they're not on fire.' Savage was 11 during filming; he was already cast in The Wonder Years TV pilot the same year.

question: Billy Mitchell achieved the first publicly-verified perfect game of Pac-Man on July 3, 1999, at a Funspot arcade in Weirs Beach NH — eating every dot, every fruit, every power pellet, and all four blue ghosts on every level through 255, then dying intentionally on the kill-screen Level 256. The session took just over six hours. What was the exact perfect score?
context: Mitchell played continuously for 6 hours and 6 minutes without losing a life. The score 3,333,360 is mathematically the maximum possible — 255 levels of 240 dots, 2 power pellets, all four ghosts and bonus fruit eaten on every level. Only a handful of perfect Pac-Man games have ever been verified since.

question: The world's largest classic-arcade museum, where Billy Mitchell achieved his perfect Pac-Man score in 1999 and where the climactic Donkey Kong duel of the King of Kong documentary takes place, is in a New Hampshire lake-resort town. Name the arcade.
choices: Pinball Hall of Fame in Las Vegas
context: Funspot was founded in 1952 by Bob Lawton. It maintains over 600 classic cabinets and is a Twin Galaxies-sanctioned official high-score recording site. The American Classic Arcade Museum within Funspot includes Pong, Computer Space, Asteroids, and dozens of working originals. The Funspot Annual Tournament has drawn world-class scorers for 40+ years.

question: The famous 'Konami Code' was first implemented by a Konami programmer who found his own game (Gradius, 1986) too hard to playtest. The code — up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A — was originally a developer cheat that gave the player full power-ups on Gradius. What was the programmer's name?
context: Hashimoto died in February 2020 at age 61. The code was supposed to be removed before retail release of Gradius but accidentally shipped. By 1988's Contra, where it gave 30 lives, it had become canon. The code appears in over 100 Konami titles plus easter-eggs across web sites, banks, and Google's old search bar.

question: In Namco's 1981 Galaga, a famous arcade-exploit lets the player make the remaining aliens stop firing entirely. The exploit requires killing all aliens except two of a specific color in a specific row, then surviving roughly 15 minutes of formation-flying without firing back. Which two aliens must remain?
answer: The two blue aliens of the bottom row
choices: The two blue aliens of the bottom row
The two red aliens of the bottom row
The two yellow flagships of the top row
The two green dragonflies in mid-formation
context: The exploit is a collision-detection bug in Galaga's enemy-state machine — Namco's programmers later acknowledged the bug had shipped. Top scorers exploit it to grind toward the 999,990 score-display rollover before continuing. The bug only works on arcade originals; most home ports patched it.

question: The 1983 Atari urban-legend cartridge dump in the New Mexico desert was excavated on April 26, 2014, by a documentary crew. The crew was led by Zak Penn — director of the resulting documentary AND screenwriter of which 2018 Spielberg adaptation that itself extensively referenced the 1983 video-game crash?
context: Penn's documentary 'Atari: Game Over' (2014) showed the excavation team finding thousands of buried Atari cartridges — including ET, Pac-Man, Centipede, Asteroids, and Defender — plus crushed manuals and console parts. The dig was sanctioned by Alamogordo NM authorities. Howard Scott Warshaw (ET's developer) attended the excavation in person.

question: Ms. Pac-Man (1982) was originally created as an unauthorized hack of Pac-Man by two students at MIT's General Computer Corporation. The original hack added a moustache, glasses, and longer legs to the protagonist. Name the two GCC engineers.
context: GCC's Macrae and Curran had already done an unauthorized speed-up hack of Missile Command (1981). They were sued by Atari and settled by becoming Atari's exclusive enhancement-kit developer.
