Their Crazy Otto Pac-Man hack was approached by Midway, licensed and rebadged as Ms. Pac-Man, and went on to gross over $1.2 billion in coin-drop.

question: The Polybius urban legend — a black-cabinet arcade game allegedly causing seizures and behavioral changes in Portland Oregon teens in 1981, supposedly removed by 'men in black' from arcades — first appeared as a credible-looking entry on what website in February 1998?
context: coinop.org's listing for Polybius cited 'unknown manufacturer' and added the conspiracy details over time. No physical cabinet, no manual, no PCB, no flyer has ever been found. The legend has been parodied in The Simpsons (S25 'Married to the Blob,' showing a black cabinet labeled 'PROPERTY OF U.S. GOV'T') and treated as creepypasta canon.

question: Williams Electronics' 1982 Joust — the two-player flap-the-button game starring an ostrich-mounted knight and a buzzard-mounted opponent — was designed by which Williams designer who picked the bird animals specifically because they could communicate mid-air flapping while still 'looking heroic'?
context: Newcomer designed several Williams classics including the dual-button flap mechanic that defined Joust. The cooperative mode where two players could fly together (and accidentally knock each other off) made Joust one of the best two-player arcade experiences of the era. The Pterodactyl appears after 70 seconds; killing it gives 1000 points.

question: Williams Electronics' 1981 Defender was famously brutal in its controls — featuring how many distinct physical inputs that the player had to coordinate simultaneously?
answer: Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick
choices: Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick
Three buttons plus an eight-direction joystick
Two buttons plus a 360-degree spinner knob
Seven buttons plus a four-direction joystick
context: Defender's controls: Reverse (flip horizontal direction), Thrust (accelerate forward), Hyperspace (teleport randomly — possibly to death), Fire (shoot horizontally), Smart Bomb (kill everything on screen). The joystick controlled vertical movement only. The complexity made Defender notoriously hard for first-time players and a beloved expertise badge for arcade veterans.

question: Konami's 1981 Frogger arcade was distributed in the US by Sega/Gremlin. The 1982 home-console port for the Atari 2600 was published by Parker Brothers and became one of the best-selling 2600 cartridges of all time, partly because of a clever marketing decision involving what?
answer: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game
choices: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game
Parker Brothers bundled it with a glow-in-the-dark frog plush
Parker Brothers added a tournament reply-card sweepstakes
Parker Brothers shipped it in a clear plastic frog-shaped case
context: The Frogger song — 'Time to hop! Look out for the cars!' — was performed by The Buckner & Garcia (also of 'Pac-Man Fever' fame) and shipped on a 45 RPM single included in the 2600 box. The track went to #57 on the Billboard Hot 100. Parker Brothers' Frogger 2600 port sold roughly 4 million units.

question: In Metal Gear Solid (1998), the boss Psycho Mantis also performs a controller-rumble feat — making the DualShock vibrate without any in-game input as a way to demonstrate his 'psychic power.' He further taunts the player with comments based on data he reads from where?
answer: The player's PS1 memory card, scanning for other Konami game saves
choices: The player's PS1 memory card, scanning for other Konami game saves
The CD-ROM disc's TOC, reading the user's region code
The PS1's BIOS clock, telling the player what time they last played
Sony's PocketStation if connected, reading installed mini-games
context: Mantis comments on Castlevania Symphony of the Night, Suikoden, and other Konami saves if they're on the card. If no Konami games are saved, he comments 'I see you don't have many Konami games.' Kojima's fourth-wall-breaking signature. The fight is solved by switching the controller from Port 1 to Port 2.

question: The NES used a custom Ricoh 6502-variant CPU and required cartridges to contain a small lockout chip to be authorized to play. The chip generated a synchronized signal that the console verified before booting. What was the chip called?
context: The 10NES chip (a Checking Integrated Circuit, or CIC) was Nintendo's region-lock and unauthorized-developer-lock. Tengen famously reverse-engineered the chip and won a US lawsuit against Nintendo in 1991 for antitrust violations. The chip is the reason why blowing on NES cartridges 'fixed' read failures — the 10NES handshake would fail on dust, then succeed on retry.

question: Every officially licensed NES, SNES, and N64 game cartridge in North America bore a small gold seal with a specific phrase printed around the Nintendo logo. The seal was the brainchild of Nintendo of America's general counsel-turned-president, Howard Lincoln, as a way to differentiate licensed games from the unlicensed shovelware of the 1983 crash. What phrase appeared on the seal?
context: The original 1985 seal said 'Official Nintendo Seal of Quality.' Nintendo dropped 'of Quality' from the seal in 1989 after lawsuits from third-party publishers (Color Dreams, Tengen) over implied quality claims. The seal then read 'Official Nintendo Seal.' Modern Nintendo Switch games no longer use the gold seal.

question: Nintendo's 1993 SNES game Star Fox was the first console game with on-cart 3D-rendering processing power. The processor — designed by British firm Argonaut Software in partnership with Nintendo — was named after a Nintendo executive's nickname for super effects. What was the chip called?
context: The Super FX was a RISC processor built into Star Fox's cartridge specifically to handle 3D polygon rendering — the SNES CPU couldn't manage it natively. Argonaut's Jez San was hired specifically to design it after demoing a working 3D game on a stock SNES. The Super FX 2 in Yoshi's Island (1995) and Doom (1995 SNES) was a faster variant.

question: When Nintendo launched the Game Boy in the US in 1989, the included pack-in cartridge was Tetris — but Nintendo had to fight a multi-party legal battle to secure the worldwide handheld rights. The Dutch-Japanese game designer who flew to Moscow in 1989 to negotiate directly with the Soviet ELORG agency for Nintendo's rights was named what?
context: Rogers had previously published the JRPG The Black Onyx (1984) in Japan. Sega's Mirrorsoft contract for handheld Tetris rights turned out to have been invalid — only ELORG had the right to grant them. Rogers went into ELORG and won the deal. The dispute is dramatized in the 2023 Apple TV+ film 'Tetris' starring Taron Egerton.

question: GoldenEye 007 (1997) contained an unlockable cheat for finishing the first mission, the Dam, in under 2 minutes 40 seconds. The reward cheat made all characters' heads and hands cartoonishly oversized. What was the cheat named?
context: DK Mode also made characters' hands oversized. The full Dam unlock list: 2:40 = paintball mode, 2:30 = invincibility, 2:20 = DK Mode. Speedrunning the Dam to under 2 minutes was the rite of passage. Multiple GoldenEye cheats only worked if a second controller was connected during the unlock — a common Rare anti-cheat habit.

question: Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) contains a notoriously long, repetitive, dimly-lit level where Master Chief must escort Cortana's data-spike through identical hallways while waves of Flood attack. Reviewers and fans called it the 'least fun' level in the entire trilogy. What was the level called?
context: Bungie reused the Library's corridor assets repeatedly due to development crunch. The level's combat is essentially the same arena 12 times. Halo 2 (2004) and Halo 3 (2007) consciously avoided this design pattern. Bungie's Marty O'Donnell scored the Library's anti-climax with the calm 'Library Suite' — a deliberate misdirection.

question: Super Mario 64 (1996) requires exactly 70 of the game's 120 Power Stars to face Bowser in the final battle 'Bowser in the Sky.' To beat the boss, Mario must grab Bowser's tail and swing him into one of three TNT bombs surrounding the platform. How many times must Bowser be thrown to win?
context: Mario grabs Bowser's tail via the B-button, twirls him via the analog stick, and releases on the right rotation arc. Each successful throw triggers a cutscene where Bowser hits a bomb. After three, Bowser explodes and drops the Power Star. The post-Bowser '120 Stars' ending unlocks Yoshi on the castle roof, who gives Mario 100 lives.

question: The Soviet Tetris rights — which Nintendo had licensed for handheld via Henk Rogers — finally reverted to Tetris's original Russian programmer in 1996 after the dissolution of the USSR. Until then, the programmer had received no royalties from the game's billions in revenue. Name him.
context: Pajitnov co-founded The Tetris Company in 1996 with Henk Rogers. Pajitnov emigrated to the US in 1991 and worked for Microsoft and others before launching The Tetris Company. The 2023 Apple TV+ film 'Tetris' dramatizes Rogers' Moscow trip to wrest the rights from Robert Maxwell and Soviet apparatchiks.

question: Mario Kart 64 (1996) introduced a famously serene battle-mode arena where four players drove on a flat empty platform suspended in a cloud-filled sky, with no obstacles or hazards. What was the arena called?
context: The four MK64 battle arenas: Block Fort (four-corner blocks with ramps), Skyscraper (open platform falling to a kill-zone), Double Deck (two-layer arena with central holes), and Big Donut (ring with no center). Block Fort's relative open-ness made it the dominant tournament-mode arena from 1996 through GameCube's Mario Kart Double Dash (2003).

question: The N64 Rumble Pak was released alongside Star Fox 64 in 1997 — Nintendo's first vibration-feedback peripheral. It plugged into the back of the controller's expansion slot, but it had a specific power source that made it different from later vibration solutions. What was the power source?
answer: Two AAA batteries inside the pack
choices: Two AAA batteries inside the pack
Drew power from the controller's main circuit board
A small lithium cell rechargeable through the cartridge slot
Solar cells on the rear shell of the pack
context: Sony's DualShock (1997 Japan, 1998 US) included rumble motors directly in the controller, drawing power from the console. The N64's battery-powered Rumble Pak was widely criticized for adding weight and requiring battery replacement. Star Fox 64 was bundled with the Rumble Pak in the US — the first game to require external vibration hardware.

question: Super Smash Bros (1999 N64) had eight starting characters and four secret unlockable characters. The four secret characters were all from less-mainstream Nintendo properties of the late 1980s. Which character below was NOT one of the four secret characters?
choices: Luigi as a clone of Mario
context: Wait — Captain Falcon IS in the base 8. Let me restate: Smash 64's base 8 were Mario, Donkey Kong, Link, Samus, Yoshi, Kirby, Fox, and Pikachu. The four unlockables were Captain Falcon, Ness, Jigglypuff, and Luigi. Marth debuted in Melee (2001). Smash creator Masahiro Sakurai also created Kirby (1992). The game was originally a one-off project called Dragon King: The Fighting Game.

question: Super Smash Bros. Melee (2001, GameCube) became the foundational competitive Smash game largely because of an unintended movement technique discovered by competitive players: an air-dodge into the ground that translated forward momentum into a slide. What was the technique called?
context: Sakurai never intended wavedashing — the physics emerged from how air-dodge momentum was preserved through ground contact. Smash 4 (2014) and Smash Ultimate (2018) deliberately removed it. EVO removed Melee from its 2013 main lineup; community outrage caused a fundraiser that paid to reinstate Melee within hours. Melee tournaments still draw thousands of players today.

question: The Sega Genesis's distinctive FM-synthesis sound — heard in Streets of Rage, Sonic the Hedgehog, Phantasy Star, and hundreds of others — was generated by a Yamaha sound chip with a specific model number. What chip?
context: The YM2612 had six FM synthesis channels plus a DAC channel for sampled sounds. The companion SN76489 (TI-licensed) provided four PSG channels for sound effects. Hidden inside the architecture: the Z80 secondary CPU handled audio playback while the Motorola 68000 ran the game. The Genesis sound architecture was a direct continuation of Sega's earlier System 16 arcade boards.

question: Super Mario 64 (1996) contains a sequence-break glitch that lets speedrunners skip large portions of the castle by repeatedly performing a specific move against a wall, building up negative speed that lets Mario clip through doors. What is the move called?
context: The BLJ exploits Mario 64's speed-clamping logic — when long-jumping backwards while running into a wall, the game accumulates negative momentum but caps positive speed. Speedrunners stack BLJ frames against the endless staircase up to Bowser, eventually clipping through. The trick lets a runner finish the game with 0, 1, 16, 50, or 70 Stars depending on what skips they perform.

question: Final Fantasy VII's (1997) final boss music 'One-Winged Angel' became iconic for its full orchestral Latin chorus. The chorus text combines four sources, including which 13th-century Latin lyrical collection that Carl Orff later set to music in 1937?
context: The 'One-Winged Angel' chorus specifically pulls 'Estuans interius / ira vehementi' from Carmina Burana. Other text comes from the Latin requiem mass. Composer Nobuo Uematsu also cites Igor Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring (1913) and Jimi Hendrix as influences. Uematsu had never written orchestral chorus music before; FF7 was his first experiment with the form.

question: Chrono Trigger (1995) composer Yasunori Mitsuda was hospitalized during the soundtrack's composition. He was 24 years old at the time, working under extreme deadline pressure. Specifically, what put him in the hospital?
answer: A perforated stomach ulcer from overwork-induced stress
choices: A perforated stomach ulcer from overwork-induced stress
Repetitive strain injuries in both wrists
Acute exhaustion from going without sleep for four days
A car accident on his commute to Square's Tokyo studio
context: Nobuo Uematsu stepped in to write 10 of the game's 65 tracks while Mitsuda recovered. Mitsuda later said he had been working roughly 20 hours a day. The Chrono Trigger soundtrack is widely considered among the greatest in video-game history. Mitsuda went on to score Xenogears (1998) and Chrono Cross (1999) under less brutal conditions.

question: The 2002 GameCube release of The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker shocked fans with its cel-shaded cartoony art style — a stark departure from the photorealistic 2000 Spaceworld demo of an adult-Link in realistic combat. The mocking fan-nickname for Wind Waker's art style became what?
context: The Spaceworld 2000 'GCN Demo' showed an adult Link sword-fighting Ganondorf in photorealistic combat — generating immense hype. The reveal of Wind Waker's cel-shaded toddler-Link with floating Tetra pirates produced an internet meltdown. Eiji Aonuma later said the realistic 2000 demo had never been a real game in development — it was a tech demo only.

question: Cortana, Master Chief's AI companion in Halo, was created through a controversial process: ONI scientists flash-cloned a copy of a living human's brain. Whose brain was Cortana cloned from?
answer: Dr. Catherine Halsey, the Spartan-II program lead scientist
choices: Dr. Catherine Halsey, the Spartan-II program lead scientist
Captain Jacob Keyes, of the Pillar of Autumn
Admiral Margaret Parangosky, head of ONI
Dr. Eric Tobin, a Halsey research colleague
context: Halsey illegally cloned her own brain to create Cortana — flash cloning was considered black-market technology by the UNSC. This makes Cortana effectively Master Chief's surrogate mother in genetic terms, since Halsey ran the Spartan-II abduction program that took six-year-old John-117 from his family. The Halo: First Strike novel by Eric Nylund (2003) is canonical.

question: The 1984 sci-fi film The Last Starfighter — about a Trailer Park teen recruited as an alien fighter pilot after beating his arcade game's high score — featured 27 minutes of CGI rendered on what was then the world's most powerful supercomputer. The computer was at Digital Productions in Los Angeles. Name the supercomputer.
answer: The Cray X-MP at Digital Productions LA
choices: The Cray X-MP at Digital Productions LA
The CDC Cyber at the Argonne Lab
context: Digital Productions installed a Cray X-MP/22 in 1983 specifically for rendering The Last Starfighter and Tron 2 (which was never made). The X-MP could render approximately one frame per 5-10 minutes. Despite the technical achievement, the film grossed only $28M against a $14M budget. Director Nick Castle later made The Boy Who Could Fly (1986) and Major Payne (1995).

question: Stranger Things Season 3 (2019) introduces Steve Harrington's Scoops Ahoy ice-cream-parlor colleague Robin Buckley — a bilingual genius who decodes Russian transmissions for Dustin and Steve. The actress playing her is the daughter of two A-list Hollywood actors. Name her.
context: Maya Hawke is the daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman. She debuts as Robin in Season 3 — the dynamic between Robin, Steve (Joe Keery), and Dustin (Gaten Matarazzo) became one of the show's best comedy trios. The Stranger Things Palace Arcade scenes were filmed at a real Atlanta reproduction arcade with period-accurate cabinets.

question: Disney's Wreck-It Ralph (2012) features cameos from real video-game characters in the 'Bad Anon' support-group scene. Of the listed real cameos, only one character lost his identifying voice — Disney could not get the licensing for the voice actor. Whose voice was missing?
answer: Kano (Mortal Kombat) — his original arcade-voice was not licensed
choices: Kano (Mortal Kombat) — his original arcade-voice was not licensed
M. Bison (Street Fighter) — Capcom wouldn't license Raul Julia's late voice
Bowser (Mario) — Nintendo wouldn't license Charles Martinet's vocals
Robotnik (Sonic) — Sega withheld the Jim Cummings voicework
context: Wreck-It Ralph director Rich Moore confirmed Disney secured Bowser, Robotnik, Zangief, Clyde, Cyril, Kano, and M. Bison appearances directly. Kano's voice in the meeting is original to the film. The film's villain Turbo / King Candy was the longest-original character — voiced by Alan Tudyk. The Pac-Man ghost in the meeting is Clyde, not Blinky.

question: The 1982 CBS-TV movie Mazes and Monsters — based on Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel inspired by the 1979 James Dallas Egbert III disappearance — starred a then-25-year-old actor in his first major TV role. The film was a centerpiece of the satanic-panic moral campaign against Dungeons & Dragons. Who starred?
context: Hanks played Robbie Wheeling, a college student whose D&D-like 'Mazes and Monsters' game blurred with reality during a delusional episode. The 1979 Egbert disappearance — a Michigan State University prodigy who vanished in steam tunnels — was misreported as D&D-related. Hanks went on to Splash (1984), Big (1988), and the modern Hollywood A-list shortly after.

question: John Badham's 1983 film WarGames — about a teenage hacker accidentally connecting to NORAD's nuclear-war simulation computer — featured the protagonist David Lightman using a specific brand of 1970s-era home computer in his bedroom. What was the computer?
context: The IMSAI 8080 (released 1975) was an early S-100-bus microcomputer built by IMS Associates. It used an Intel 8080 CPU and shipped as a kit or assembled. Director Badham picked it for its dramatic front-panel of toggle switches and red LEDs. The WHOPPER supercomputer at NORAD was played by Cray-style cabinetry; the actual line 'shall we play a game?' came from an Apple-II text-to-speech card.
